A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same multi-agent inverse reinforcement learning work, despite v3's revised title and substantial theoretical expansion. The complete text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support comparison.

before.justification: Section 6 and Appendix F report original gridworld experiments comparing reward recovery with behavior cloning, including transfer results and an empirical comparison with the theoretical bound.

after.justification: Appendix F retains the original gridworld experiments and Nash-gap results comparing reward recovery with behavior cloning.

M1.justification: v3 introduces entropy-regularized reward recovery involving log-policy and opponent-policy terms, substantially extending the inference formulation. Its pure-NE Algorithm 1 also removes repeated expert-policy updates and uses revised transition-only uncertainty. The experimental Random Max Gap procedure remains unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same two-agent 3 × 3 gridworld, with deterministic training and transfer to stochastic-transition and obstacle environments. The new Stag-Hunt examples are analytical illustrations, not additional training or evaluation coverage.

E2.justification: Behavior cloning remains the evaluated comparison method in Figure 1. NashQ-Learning still generates expert policies rather than serving as an additional baseline. Newly cited methods are not experimentally compared.

E3.justification: The retained experiments use the same environment construction, expert generation, transition scenarios, Nash-gap metric, and sample axis. The new pure-NE and QRE assumptions concern theoretical analysis; no revised experimental settings are reported.

E4.justification: v1 Appendix F.3's diagnostic comparing the theoretical bound with empirical Nash gaps is removed. The stochastic-transition and obstacle-transfer analyses remain unchanged, so this is a limited reduction in supplementary analysis.

E5.justification: The uncertainty construction for reward estimation changes substantially: v3 replaces stochastic-support bounds in the pure-NE analysis and adds log-policy, total-variation, and reciprocal-probability bounds for QRE recovery in Appendices D and G. These are analytical guarantees, not additional experimental runs. The explicit confidence-interval clipping discussion accompanying v1 Figure 3 is also removed.

E6.justification: Figure 1's plotted results and comparison with behavior cloning are identical. v3 removes Figure 3's empirical-gap and theoretical-bound curves, together with the reported finding that the theoretical bound substantially exceeds the observed gap.

T1.justification: v3 restricts the original explicit characterization and unregularized sample-complexity result to pure Nash experts, allows signed rewards, and revises bounded-reward arguments. Sections 5–7 and Appendices D, E, and G add equilibrium-ambiguity examples, an all-equilibria feasible-set definition, QRE characterizations and proofs, a bound involving Delta_min^-4, and identifiability derivations under reward separability.

C1.justification: The abstract, contributions, and conclusion shift from general Nash-expert characterization and sampling guarantees toward the insufficiency of single-equilibrium observations. v3 narrows the original characterization to pure equilibria and adds central claims about entropy regularization resolving equilibrium selection and sample-complexity guarantees for QRE experts.

C2.justification: v1 mainly discusses differing equilibrium values to motivate the Nash gap. v3 develops the stronger limitation that feasible rewards can change the game's strategic structure or equilibria, explains why regularized policies constrain rewards differently, and discusses conditional identifiability. It removes the earlier explanation of the empirical bound's looseness and inefficient exploration in Appendix F.3.

D1.justification: Removing Appendix F.3 also removes the explicit disclosure that the gridworld has 72 possible states. The retained environment description, NashQ expert-generation information, and Random Max Gap optimization remain substantially unchanged; no code, hardware, or runtime information is added.

R1.justification: v1 Appendix B's extensive survey of forward-MARL complexity results is removed. v3 substantially develops positioning around regularization and identifiability, including Cao et al., Rolland et al., Leonardos et al., and Savas et al., and adds discussion of offline IRL and newer multi-agent imitation work.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, contribution list, related work, and conclusion are substantially rewritten. The original characterization and sampling narrative is condensed into Section 4, new Sections 5–7 organize the expanded argument, and experimental material moves into Appendix F. The appendix structure is reorganized and its contents list removed.

P2.justification: v3 adds Stag-Hunt payoff tables, relocates Figure 1 and Algorithm 1 to the appendices, and removes Figure 3. Figure 1's display, the gridworld diagrams, and the notation table are otherwise retained within the same general page design.

improvement.justification: v3 usefully exposes equilibrium ambiguity and qualifies the original characterization to pure equilibria, but removes the empirical bound diagnostic. Its new central theory also contains unresolved inconsistencies: Lemma D.4 bounds a reciprocal probability product by a quantity tending to zero, whereas Lemma G.4 bounds a difference of reciprocals. These issues affect the new sample-complexity argument, preventing a reliable net quality assessment.
